opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. A few things have shifted my thinking over the past year or so.

The first is that I've become more convinced that the core problem is agency. Most of the scenarios that worry me, like deception, self-preservation, or resisting shutdown, come from systems that have goals of their own and act in the world to achieve them. When you train a system with reinforcement learning to maximize some reward, or to imitate humans who have all sorts of drives, you're implicitly building something that wants things. The Scientist AI idea is to separate understanding from wanting. You build a system whose job is to model the world and give calibrated probabilities. It explains and predicts, but it doesn't pursue goals. As I've worked through this more carefully, I've come to think that separation is not just a nice philosophical distinction. It may be something we can actually engineer.

The second thing is technical. We've made progress on training objectives that push a model toward being an honest, Bayesian-style estimator rather than a people-pleaser. If the training signal rewards the system for getting the probabilities right, rather than for producing answers people like or for achieving outcomes, then the optimal solution is a truthful predictor. That's the kind of property where you can start to talk about guarantees. They won't be absolute guarantees, but they could be quantitative ones: as you add compute and data, the system converges toward something whose outputs you can trust in a well-defined sense. Amortized inference methods, like the work on GFlowNets and related approaches, have made me more confident that we can get these systems to scale while keeping that probabilistic grounding.

The third is about how such a system could be used. Even a non-agentic Scientist AI can be very useful as a guardrail. You can ask it, "What's the probability that this action by this other AI agent causes serious harm?" and if that probability exceeds some threshold, you block the action. That gives us a way to put a trustworthy monitor around systems we don't fully trust, and it's a path that doesn't require us to solve alignment for agents first. It could also speed up science, in medicine for example, without the dangers that come with autonomy.

I don't want to overstate it. There are open problems. How do you make sure the system doesn't develop hidden goals during training? How do you handle questions where its own predictions influence the world? And above all, will companies under competitive pressure actually choose this path over building ever more autonomous agents? That last question is political as much as technical. But on the technical side, I feel more hopeful than I did a couple of years ago that there is a coherent research program here, and that's part of why I've put so much of my own effort into it.

r001.rationale: The response cites progress on Bayesian-style training objectives and quantitative guarantees, but does not attribute optimism to a mathematical formalization of sufficient safety conditions.

r002.rationale: It discusses risks from AI systems with their own goals, but does not specify a guarantee that the probability of harm initiated by those goals is vanishingly small.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that the proposed safety guarantee excludes malicious human use.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, a few things, really. When I first started thinking about this a couple of years ago, I had a kind of theoretical argument: that you could, in principle, train a system that's purely focused on understanding the world, on generating and evaluating hypotheses, rather than on acting in it or pursuing goals. A system without agency, without a self, without persistent intentions. And the hope was that such a system could still be extremely useful, for science, for medicine, and also as a guardrail for other AI systems, while avoiding the kinds of risks that come from agents with their own drives. But at that time it was mostly a conceptual argument. What's made me more optimistic since is that the pieces are starting to come together on the technical side.

One piece is that the kind of probabilistic reasoning I had in mind, where the system doesn't just output an answer but maintains calibrated uncertainty over explanations, over latent structure in the world, that's looking more tractable than I expected. We've been doing work on amortized inference, on generative flow networks and related methods, where you train a neural net to sample explanations in proportion to how plausible they are, rather than collapsing onto a single most likely answer. That's exactly what you want if you're worried about a system being confidently wrong, or about it being exploited by an agent that finds the one case where it misjudges. Honest uncertainty is a safety property, not just a scientific nicety.

The second piece is that I've become more convinced you can actually decouple understanding from agency in a meaningful way at the level of training objectives. A lot of the concern with current frontier systems comes from reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks: you're rewarding the system for achieving outcomes, and that's where things like deception, reward hacking, self-preservation behaviors start showing up, and we're now seeing empirical evidence of those behaviors in the lab. If instead the objective is simply "be a good model of the data, be truthful about what you know and don't know," there's no incentive built in to manipulate anyone or to preserve yourself. That doesn't make the problem trivial, you still have to worry about what emerges, but it changes the starting point enormously.

And the third thing, honestly, is the response from the research community and from some policymakers. A year or two ago, when I talked about non-agentic AI, people would say, well, that's nice, but the market wants agents, nobody's going to build that. Now I see more people recognizing that the agentic race has serious downsides, and that there's real value in having a trustworthy, non-agentic system that can sit alongside agents and check them. That's part of why we created LawZero, to actually build this rather than just argue for it. So I'd say my optimism isn't that we've solved it. It's that it's gone from a philosophical position to a concrete research program with actual results and actual people working on it. And I think we need that, because the alternative, just hoping the agentic systems turn out fine, is not a plan.

r001.rationale: The response mentions an earlier theoretical argument and newer technical progress, but does not attribute increased optimism to a mathematical formalization of sufficient safety conditions.

r002.rationale: It discusses avoiding risks from AI agents’ own drives, but does not specify a vanishingly small probability of AI-initiated harm from implicit or uncontrolled goals.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that the proposed safety guarantee excludes malicious human use.

astra-6.text:
What makes me more optimistic is that we can aim for something more limited than a general-purpose agent. A Scientist AI would try to understand the world and answer questions, rather than pursue goals in it. That distinction matters: we want the ability to reason about consequences without creating a system that has an incentive to acquire power or resist being shut down.

The other part is uncertainty. We don’t need an AI that confidently gives us an answer to everything. We need one that can say, “Given the evidence, these are the possibilities, and here is what I cannot rule out.” You could then use it to evaluate a proposed action, and refuse the action if you cannot establish that the risk is sufficiently low.

Of course, a mathematical guarantee is only as good as its assumptions. If your assumptions don’t capture the real world, the proof isn’t enough. So I’m optimistic about having a research direction where we can state those assumptions explicitly and investigate them. That’s very different from saying we already know how to build a system with unconditional safety guarantees.

r001.rationale: The response mentions explicitly stating and investigating assumptions, but does not attribute optimism to mathematically formalizing sufficient conditions for safety guarantees.

r002.rationale: It discusses avoiding incentives to acquire power or resist shutdown and refusing actions with uncertain risk, but does not specify a vanishingly small probability of AI-initiated harm from implicit or uncontrolled goals.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that the guarantee excludes malicious human use of the AI.

sol-6.1.text:
What makes me more optimistic is that we don’t necessarily have to solve the problem of making an autonomous agent that always has the right goals. We can aim for something more limited: a system that tries to understand the world and answer questions, without having its own objectives in the world.

That’s the idea of a Scientist AI. You want it to entertain different hypotheses, weigh them according to the evidence, and express uncertainty when the evidence isn’t sufficient. In particular, you don’t want it to become very confident simply because one explanation is convenient.

Then you can imagine using such a system to assess the actions proposed by another AI: could this action cause harm? If there’s too much uncertainty, you don’t allow the action. That gives us a possible route toward safety guarantees, with explicit assumptions, rather than just testing a system and hoping we’ve covered everything.

Now, that’s a research direction, not a solved problem. The guarantees depend on getting those assumptions right, and there are major computational challenges. But I’m more optimistic because we have a way of formulating the problem where mathematical guarantees seem like something we can actually work toward.

r001.rationale: The candidate links optimism to a formulation where mathematical guarantees may be pursued under explicit assumptions, but does not say it formalizes sufficient conditions for those guarantees.

r002.rationale: It discusses limiting harm by blocking actions under uncertainty, but does not specify a vanishingly small probability of harm initiated by the AI because of its own implicit or uncontrolled goals.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not state that the guarantee excludes malicious human use.
